sections.heading: Title
sections.source_text: Gravitational-wave parameter estimation has traditionally leaned on a convenient fiction: that detector noise is Gaussian and stationary. Real instruments like LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA break that assumption with glitches, spectral lines, and drifting sensitivity. This work, from a Montréal and Flatiron Institute team, introduces Score-based Likelihood Characterization, or SLIC. Instead of assuming a noise model, they train a score-based diffusion model to learn the real noise distribution directly from detector data, then combine it with a differentiable physical waveform model to build an unbiased likelihood. On a simulated signal injected into real LIGO noise, SLIC recovers the true source parameters with high credibility, pointing toward accurate and scalable gravitational-wave inference free of idealized noise assumptions.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.source_text: Extracting astrophysics from gravitational-wave detectors requires Bayesian inference over source parameters like black hole masses and spins, and that inference needs a likelihood. For decades the field has assumed detector noise is Gaussian and stationary, because it makes the likelihood tractable and cheap. But real detectors are messy. Their sensitivity evolves over time, and their data are contaminated by transient bursts called glitches and by narrow, wandering spectral features called lines. There are no generative models for most of these contaminants, so today they are handled segment by segment with custom fixes that are costly and can introduce bias. The most famous example was the first binary neutron star merger, GW170817, which landed right on top of a loud glitch in a LIGO detector.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.source_text: Why does this matter now? Because gravitational-wave astronomy is scaling up fast. Analyzing large collections of signals makes the whole pipeline sensitive even to tiny departures from Gaussian noise, and those departures quietly accumulate into biases. The authors wanted a way to keep the advantages of the deterministic waveform models that standard inference relies on, while dropping the unrealistic assumption about the noise. That would let them analyze signals contaminated by artifacts without bespoke data surgery, and prepare for next-generation detectors like Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope, which will record vastly more events.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.source_text: The core contribution is to bring a technique called Score-based Likelihood Characterization, or SLIC, to gravitational-wave inference. The idea, originally developed for astronomical imaging with Hubble and Webb, is to learn the score of the noise distribution with a diffusion model instead of assuming its form. The authors couple that learned noise score with a differentiable physical waveform model to produce an unbiased estimate of the likelihood. They then show two things end to end: that the model can generate realistic synthetic LIGO noise, capturing even sharp spectral lines, and that its likelihood recovers the true parameters of a simulated signal injected into real detector data.

sections.heading: Method
sections.source_text: Here is how SLIC works. The setting is an inverse problem with additive noise: an observation equals a deterministic signal model plus noise. If you can learn the score of the noise distribution, meaning the gradient of its log probability, you can construct the score of the likelihood. So the authors train a score-based diffusion model on samples of real LIGO noise using denoising score matching, learning that gradient with respect to the data. They then chain it with the Jacobian of a differentiable waveform model. For the physics they use the differentiable IMRPhenomD waveform implemented in the ripple package, which makes automatic differentiation of the waveform, and hence the required Jacobian, possible. During inference the noise enters as the residual between the observation and the model. To draw samples from the resulting likelihood they use Langevin dynamics, specifically a Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm called MALA.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.source_text: The demonstration uses real detector data. The team trains the score-based network on eleven hours of actual LIGO-Hanford data recorded around the GW150914 event, sampled at four thousand ninety-six hertz and split into four-second segments, carefully discarding the one segment that contains the true historical signal. Training happens in the Fourier domain after applying a Tukey window. To test the method, they inject a simulated signal with parameters consistent with GW150914 into a stretch of real LIGO noise recorded after the training window and never seen during training. That injected signal has a chirp mass of twenty-nine solar masses, a symmetric mass ratio near 0.25, zero spins, and a luminosity distance of four hundred megaparsecs, mimicking a standard real analysis.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.source_text: The results are encouraging. First, the authors draw one thousand twenty-four noise realizations from SLIC and compare their power spectrum to a Welch estimate from real LIGO data. The two agree closely, and remarkably the learned model resolves the narrow spectral lines even more finely than the Welch estimate, because it was trained on eleven hours of data versus one hour for the empirical estimate. Second, they inject a known signal and infer its parameters with both SLIC and a standard Gaussian likelihood. SLIC recovers all five varied parameters with high credibility, and its posterior is actually tighter, with smaller variance, than the Gaussian-likelihood posterior on this clean segment.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.source_text: The paper's key comparison is against the conventional approach. For the injected signal, they run inference twice: once with their learned SLIC likelihood, and once with a standard Gaussian likelihood built from a Welch power spectral density. They deliberately chose a segment of real data without significant glitches, so that even the Gaussian likelihood recovers the true parameters. Both methods succeed on this clean case, which validates SLIC against the trusted baseline, but the SLIC posterior comes out with smaller variance, hinting at the gains expected once the method is applied to genuinely non-Gaussian, glitch-contaminated data.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.source_text: A few numbers anchor the demonstration. The score model is trained on eleven hours of real LIGO-Hanford noise around GW150914. Validation of the learned noise draws on one thousand twenty-four synthetic noise realizations, whose power spectrum matches the real data. Inference recovers five source parameters: the chirp mass, the symmetric mass ratio, the luminosity distance, the coalescence time, and the coalescence phase. The data are sampled at four thousand ninety-six hertz in four-second segments, and the injected test signal has a chirp mass of twenty-nine solar masses at a distance of four hundred megaparsecs.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.source_text: The takeaway is that you no longer have to assume the noise is Gaussian and stationary. By learning the real noise distribution with a diffusion model and coupling it to a differentiable waveform, SLIC produces an unbiased likelihood directly from detector data, and it recovers true parameters on real LIGO noise. The current version is a proof of concept, limited to four-second single-detector segments and a simple MALA sampler. The authors are already extending it to longer segments for neutron-star signals, to coherent multi-detector analysis, and to more powerful samplers like flowMC. With those pieces in place, machine-learning noise models could enable fast, scalable, and unbiased inference for future gravitational-wave observations.
